title_original: Eva Besnyö: A Life Outside the Frame
excerpt_original: At the Fotomuseum Den Haag, “The Liberated Camera” retraces the path of this Hungarian-born photographer who embraced modernism in Berlin, escaped the Nazis and found a second wind in the Dutch women’s movement. L’article Eva Besnyö: A Life Outside the Frame est apparu en…

blocks.text: On a tree-lined path in Balatonlelle, Hungary, in the summer of 1931, a boy walks away from the camera with a double bass strapped to his back. The instrument is almost as large as he is; its diagonal cuts across the verticals of the trees. We never see his face. The photograph, taken by Eva Besnyö, then twenty-one, quickly became her most reproduced image: circulated by Neofot, a Berlin agency, printed in newspapers and magazines, later turned into postcards and even a puzzle, often without her name and wrapped in a soft romantic haze.

Besnyö would later remark that people always brought up “this little boy” when they thought of her. “In a way, he has become my trademark.” The retrospective now on view at the Fotomuseum Den Haag restores what the romantic framing erased: the boy was a working child, helping to support his family by playing an instrument with a missing string. Built around the museum’s recent acquisition of 341 prints once held by Besnyö’s daughter, the show places this image and some two hundred others back into the life, and the political weather, that produced them.

blocks.caption: Boy with bass , Balatonlelle, Hungary, 1931 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.alt: Man lifting a child against the sky, Balatonlelle, 1931, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: Paul Beck holding Bobby Kirchner , Balatonlelle, Hungary, 1931 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.text: Budapest, Berlin, Amsterdam: Besnyö’s life thus follows the fault lines of the 20th century. Born in 1910 into a prosperous Jewish family in Budapest, she trained with József Pécsi (1889-1956) and absorbed the sharp-eyed modernism of Albert Renger-Patzsch and his book Die Welt ist schön (“The World Is Beautiful”). In 1930 she left for Berlin, then the most vital photographic city in Europe. The self-portrait she made the following year, holding her Rolleiflex and looking straight into the lens with cropped hair and steady gaze, already announces the stance she would later call “the liberated camera”: the freedom to photograph whatever one saw or needed to express, unburdened by painterly convention.

Berlin would prove decisive. She arrived without homesickness and threw herself into the city’s experimental climate. With friends she watched films by Eisenstein and Pudovkin, studying their visual language. She worked for studios and press agencies to fund her own darkroom, while testing the formal possibilities of what became known as New Photography, or New Vision, championed by László Moholy-Nagy (1895-1946). The movement treated the camera as a tool for revealing the world in a new, objective and experimental way. Unexpected angles, strong diagonals, clean and uncluttered compositions: Besnyö absorbed these principles completely. With a keen eye she photographed people, cities, architecture and the rapid social changes around her, presenting the modern world as dynamic and constantly in flux.

blocks.alt: Eva Besnyö self-portrait holding a Rolleiflex camera, Berlin, 1931
blocks.caption: Self-portrait with Rolleiflex camera , Berlin, 1931 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.alt: Portrait of artist and designer György Kepes, Berlin, 1931, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: Artist and designer György Kepes , Berlin, 1931 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.text: One negative of Starnberger Straße, shot from above onto the street corner, its pavements and its passers-by, appears in the exhibition in two different prints. In the 1930s she cropped it tightly; decades later she preferred a wider frame that kept the solitary walker near the edge. “That gives the photo much more tension,” she would later say. “That, too, is part of your evolution as a photographer.” Hanging the two versions side by side is one of the exhibition’s quietest, and most perceptive, curatorial choices.

Besnyö also helped others find their way. Her childhood neighbor from Budapest, Endre Friedmann, followed her to Berlin. When he hesitated about becoming a photographer, she told him it demanded everything. She later secured him a job in the lab of DEPHOT, one of the first photo agencies. He would soon be known by another name: Robert Capa.

blocks.alt: High-angle view of a Berlin street corner with passers-by and a car, 1931, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: Starnberger Straße , Berlin, 1931 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.text: By 1932, the rise of Nazism had made Berlin untenable for a young Jewish woman. She followed John Fernhout, a Dutch filmmaker and photographer she would marry the following year, to the Netherlands. What first struck her as provincial soon became a network: the painter Charley Toorop (Fernhout’s mother), the photographer Carel Blazer, the architect Alexander Bodon. She photographed modern architecture with evident pleasure (concrete, steel, glass, the clean volumes of the New Building movement) and quickly gained recognition. Her first solo exhibition, at the Kunstzaal Van Lier in Amsterdam in 1933, confirmed it.

Beauty, however, was no longer enough. After arriving in the Netherlands, Besnyö came under the influence of socially engaged documentary photography that focused on poverty, labour and inequality. Images were no longer meant to be simply beautiful; they were expected to carry a society-changing message. This idea shaped her street and documentary work, as in her photograph of a group of working-class men standing in the street, presumably unemployed, as if to refuse any romanticization and record instead the quiet weight of economic hardship.

blocks.alt: Modernist summer house interior opening onto fields, Groet, 1934, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: The Dijkstra family’s summer house, architects Merkelbach and Karsten , Groet, 1934 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.alt: Six women stretching on a mat seen from above, Amsterdam, 1933, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: Gymnastics lesson by Chaja Goldstein , Amsterdam, 1933 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.text: Her talent for organization found its fullest expression in 1937, with “Foto ’37,” an ambitious exhibition at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. Officially, the committee was chaired by Paul Schuitema, with Besnyö listed as secretary. In practice, she did much of the heavy lifting: drawing on her international contacts, she gathered some 1,500 photographs and wrote the wall texts. “We wanted to show that photography had become an inextricable part of everyday life,” she wrote. Reportage, advertising, portraiture, even X-rays: all had their place on the walls. A landmark in establishing photography’s seriousness within the Dutch museum world, and a cause she would pursue for the rest of her life.

“Besnyö had not only an exceptional talent for photography, but strong entrepreneurial instincts as well,” notes Margriet Schavemaker, general director of the Kunstmuseum Den Haag and the Fotomuseum Den Haag. “From her position as a migrant, she managed time and again to earn a place for herself in leading artistic circles; to build her own career through photo commissions; and to carry out initiatives that advanced photography as an artform, such as the groundbreaking ‘Foto ’37’ exhibition in the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam.”

The war interrupted everything. In 1942 she went into hiding, obtained false papers, and for a time photographed for forged documents. With the help of friends and her mother, she succeeded in 1944 in having the “J” for Jew removed from her identity papers. That same year, her father was deported to Auschwitz and murdered.

blocks.alt: Portrait of Pauline Citroen in a lace shawl by a window, Amsterdam, 1954, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: Pauline Citroen , Amsterdam, 1954 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.text: Peace then brought another kind of confinement. After the liberation, Besnyö tried to resume her career while starting a family with the graphic designer Wim Brusse; their son, Berthus, was born in 1945, their daughter, Iara, in 1948. She was overjoyed to have children, but doing everything at once proved far harder. In the deeply conservative Netherlands of the 1950s, sharing childcare and work equally with her husband was out of reach, and the independence she had taken for granted as a young woman slipped away. Even the inclusion of one of her photographs in “The Family of Man,” Edward Steichen’s (1879-1973) monumental exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1955, changed nothing at home. She described the particular isolation of the housewife who can no longer follow the conversation when friends visit: “I found that symptomatic of housewives, that you’re held back in your mental development.”

It would take until the 1970s, with her children grown and her marriage over, for Besnyö to recover a public role that matched the independence of her early career. She joined the radical feminist action group Dolle Mina and photographed its protests with the same alertness she had once brought to Berlin streets and Dutch construction sites. At one action in Amsterdam in 1976, activists in white coats wore placards reading “Terug naar de breinaald” (“Back to the knitting needle”), a bitter allusion to backstreet abortions at a time when the right to abortion was still being fought over in the Netherlands. Besnyö was there with her camera. The woman who had fought in the 1930s to have photography taken seriously in museums now used that same medium to document the struggle for women’s emancipation. Less a late conversion than a reconnection: the “liberated camera” she had celebrated in her twenties found a new subject in the demand that women themselves be liberated from the roles that had constrained her.

blocks.alt: Dolle Mina activists in white coats with placards, Amsterdam, 1976, by Eva Besnyö
blocks.caption: Protest by the feminist action group Dolle Mina: “Back to the knitting needle” , Amsterdam, 1976 © Eva Besnyö / Maria Austria Instituut

blocks.text: Besnyö died in 2003, at ninety-three, still campaigning for photography’s place in Dutch museums and still putting her own archive in order. “The Liberated Camera,” the largest survey of her work to date, does not make a heroine of her; it follows, print by print and document by document, a century of migration, modernism, persecution and hard-won independence. The boy with the bass is still there, but as one image among two hundred. And the 341 prints at the heart of the show now belong to a Dutch museum: precisely the kind of institution Besnyö spent her life urging to take photography seriously.
The exhibition “The Liberated Camera,” by Eva Besnyö, is on view at Fotomuseum Den Haag , in The Hague, from September 5, 2026, to January 31, 2027.
Eva Besnyö: The Liberated Camera , the accompanying book, is published by Hannibal Books and available for €64.50.
